title: Incremental stitching and tool scopes: hosted SDK proposal
content:
Overview:

This note documents a pragmatic PRD-level proposal for a compact session protocol that enables incremental stitching of partial model outputs with deterministic tool-scoping semantics and a slim SDK handshake for embedded clients. Goal is to reduce integration friction for customers who need: low-latency progressive results, sound tool invocation boundaries, and reproducible structured outputs for downstream systems (search indexing, CRMs, downstream pipelines).

Why this is different:
- Many of our hosted-api drafts focus on large, feature-complete streaming protocols. This doc explores a small-footprint, opinionated client surface that trades generality for predictable upgrade paths and easier server-side guarantees.
- Introduces the concept of "tool scopes": explicit tubular boundaries around tool invocations that carry minimal metadata and a monotonic progression token to enable safe stitching and replay.

Success criteria (measurable):
- Integration time: reduce median integration time for SDK embedding by 40% vs current baseline (tracked via support intake).
- Latency: 95th percentile first-byte latency for incremental fragments under 300ms for common mobile + web flows.
- Reliability: fewer than 1% resume/replay errors across canary customers during rollout.
- Observability: per-session replay token and per-tool-call counters available in Console for debugs.

Non-goals:
- Not attempting to standardize every streaming corner-case (full transactional tool graphs, multi-client synchronous editing).
- Not replacing the full-featured streaming surface for heavy integrations; this is an alternative ergonomics target.

User personas and stories:
- Mobile-first product engineer: wants partial answers quickly while reserving tool calls for critical steps. Example: preview summary appears within 150ms, heavy tool call (DB query) happens after user taps "expand".
- Platform engineer at enterprise: wants deterministic logs for auditing tool invocations and to be able to replay session fragments into a staging replica.
- Developer building a multi-step assistant: needs typed outputs (JSON simplified schema) so downstream systems can consume without custom parsing.

Key primitives (proposal):
1) Session token + monotonic fragment indices
- Each session is allocated a short opaque token by the server on session creation.
- Each incremental fragment emitted by the model runtime is annotated with an integer fragment_idx (0..n). Fragments are idempotent and replayable by index.

2) Tool scope envelope
- Tool calls are published as "tool-scope" frames that include: scope_id (uuid), tool_name, minimal schema reference (string id), trigger_fragment_idx (the fragment index that requested the tool), and optional hint metadata (cost_tier, estimated-latency).
- Tool-scope frames are separate from textual fragments; they may arrive in-stream or as a side-channel event, but they share the same fragment_idx space so clients can stitch deterministically.

3) Incremental stitching rules (client guidance)
- Clients render textual fragments as they arrive. When a tool-scope frame is received with trigger_fragment_idx == k, client should:
  a) Commit text fragments up to index k as the baseline.
  b) Render a lightweight placeholder UI for the tool call (spinner with tool_name and hint).
  c) When the tool result fragment arrives (it has a later fragment_idx), merge by simple append or by applying a lightweight patch token described below.

4) Minimal patch token for structured edits
- To support deterministic small edits (replace, insert at position, annotate-span) the server may emit a patch token referencing the baseline fragment_idx, operation (replace|insert|annotate), and a byte-range or token-range. The token is intentionally small; clients may choose to ignore patches and fall back to full-fragment replace.

5) Typed-output schema references
- Rather than inlining full JSON schemas in every fragment, the server will reference schema ids (hosted in Model Catalog). Clients can request schema definitions on-demand. This keeps fragment payloads small while enabling structured validation for consumers that need it.

SDK ergonomics: surface and handshake
- SDK surface (JavaScript + mobile): lightweight SessionClient with three primary methods:
  - openSession({model, schemaOptIn, preferIncremental}) -> session_token
  - onFragment(callback(fragment_idx, type, payload, metadata)) -> subscription
  - sendInput({session_token, content, metadata}) -> ack

- Handshake: openSession returns: session_token, initial_fragment_idx (usually 0), offered_features (list, e.g., ["tool-scopes","patch-tokens","schema-ref"]). Client picks features they support in an opt-in manner.

Backpressure and bandwidth modes
- SDK exposes a mode flag: prefer_latency | prefer_bandwidth. When prefer_bandwidth is set, the server may coalesce small fragments and emit fewer, larger fragments; prefer_latency prioritizes immediate small fragments.
- For unstable networks, SDK will support a compact delta replay mode where clients can request fragments by index to recover gaps.

Observability and debugging
- Every fragment and tool-scope frame is logged with session_token, fragment_idx, trace_id, and a compact fingerprint of model variant (model_id:quantized_flag).
- Console will expose a per-session trace with timeline view: fragments (text), tool-scopes (metadata), and patches.

Security and auditability
- Tool scope frames will include an optional signed assertion for enterprise Private deployments to provide non-repudiable audit trails (HMAC over scope_id + trigger_fragment_idx).
- Schema definitions are versioned; when a schema changes, model catalog will issue a schema_version. Session handshake must include schema_version compatibility check.

Compatibility matrix and fallback model behavior
- For clients that do not support tool-scopes, server falls back to inlining tool results as plain fragments marked with legacy_tool_marker.
- For older clients that do not understand patch tokens, server must ensure a full-fragment replace is available (patch tokens are optional optimization).

Rollout plan (canary -> gradual):
1) Internal eng + SE testbed (2 wks): SDK + server switch with opt-in feature flags.
2) Beta customers (selected) for 1 month: monitor first-byte latencies and replay errors.
3) General availability with Console traces turned on for all sessions.

Metrics to track:
- fragment_rate (fragments/sec) and avg bytes per fragment
- first_fragment_latency P50/P95
- tool-scope-to-result round-trip (ms)
- resume_requests per 1000 sessions (gap recovery)
- schema_mismatch_rate (sessions that requested schema but got incompatible version)

Open questions and tradeoffs:
- Patch token expressivity: How rich do we allow operations? Minimal ops reduce client complexity but may require larger fragments.
- Tool chaining semantics: Should tool scopes support reactive chains (tool A triggers tool B) with transactional guarantees, or keep them single-step for simplicity?
- Client-side merging: how much responsibility do we place on SDK vs app for applying patches and UI transitions?

Implementation notes for engineering:
- Server: extend streaming protocol to include frame_type enum {TEXT_FRAGMENT, TOOL_SCOPE, PATCH_TOKEN, SESSION_CONTROL}. Keep wire compact (small integer tags).
- Persistence: fragments must be stored in append-only log per session with fragment_idx as index to support replay by index.
- Catalog: schema store with schema_id -> JSON Schema + version metadata, accessible via a CDN for low-latency retrieval.

Next steps and owner map:
- Define precise wire encoding for frames (binary vs json) — owner: Markus Chen — 2 weeks
- SDK API prototype (JS + iOS) with simple UI demo — owner: Priya Kapoor — 3 weeks
- Server append-only session log and replay endpoints — owner: Ethan Blake — 3 weeks
- Console trace view prototype — owner: Lina Rodriguez (PM) — 4 weeks

Appendix: sample fragment timeline (illustrative)
- fragment_idx=0: "User: draft of question"
- fragment_idx=1: TEXT_FRAGMENT: "Assistant: short preview summary"
- fragment_idx=2: TOOL_SCOPE: {scope_id: S-1, tool_name: "db_query", trigger_fragment_idx:1} 
- fragment_idx=3: TEXT_FRAGMENT: "Assistant: continuing with caveat -> will call db"
- fragment_idx=4: TEXT_FRAGMENT (tool result merged): "Assistant: final answer with results"

The sample shows how clients can render preview content and reserve a deterministic slot for the tool result, reducing flicker and preventing repeated tool re-invocations on reconnects.

If this approach looks promising, we should convert this note into a lightweight PRD with diagrams (timeline, handshake flow, wire layout) and a small API surface spec for the SDKs.
